abstract.text: We focus on the utilisation of reactive trajectory imitation controllers for goal-directed mobile robot navigation. We propose a topological navigation graph (TNG) - an imitationlearning-based framework for navigating through environments with intersecting trajectories. The TNG framework represents the environment as a directed graph composed of deep neural networks. Each vertex of the graph corresponds to a trajectory and is represented by a trajectory identification classifier and a trajectory imitation controller. For trajectory following, we propose the novel use of neural object detection architectures. The edges of TNG correspond to intersections between trajectories and are all represented by a classifier. We provide empirical evaluation of the proposed navigation framework and its components in simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating that TNG allows us to utilise non-goal-directed, imitation-learning methods for goal-directed autonomous navigation.

source_span.start_text: Combining perception and action into a single algorithm of fundamental and practical importance, mobile robot navigation is an attractive area for artificial intelligence research.

sections.summary: Motivates the need for goal-directed navigation from imitation-learning components. Reviews the limitations of probabilistic-geometric models and the promise of neural-network imitation learning, then identifies the core problem that many imitation-learning algorithms are not goal-directed by design. Introduces the TNG framework as the solution and lists the paper’s main contributions.
sections.title: Introduction: Goal-Directed Navigation from Imitation Learning

source_span.end_text: The error input for the PID controller is defined as e t:= x t − x c, where x t and x c are the detected bounding box’s centre x coordinate and the centre x coordinate of the input image (see Figure 3).
source_span.start_text: In this section, we focus on learning a reactive skill of visuomotor trajectory following independently from the overall navigation method.

sections.summary: Defines the trajectory-following skill and presents two reactive controllers. The regression controller uses a fixed CNN encoder with a trainable MLP, ridge regression, DAgger, and augmentation; its limitations are rotational error sensitivity, environmental sensitivity, and weak correlation between offline loss and execution. The object-detection-based controller uses RetinaNet to detect the direction of movement as a single-class bounding box, then a PID controller centers the box.
sections.title: Trajectory Imitation Controllers: Regression and Object Detection

source_span.start_text: In this section, we review similar work of other authors and formally describe the proposed TNG framework for creating a goal-driven navigation system from separately learnt reactive skills.

sections.summary: Reviews related navigation approaches: mapper-planner end-to-end methods, semi-parametric topological memory, and kilometre-scale reinforcement-learning navigation. Critiques their resource demands, assumptions, or lack of real-world demonstrations. Then formally defines TNG as a directed graph whose vertices are trajectory imitation controllers plus trajectory classifiers and whose edges are intersection classifiers. Describes localisation, goal identification, shortest-path planning, switching, and goal reaching.
sections.title: Topological Navigation Graph: Prior Work and Formal Framework

source_span.start_text: Trajectory classifiers g(X|φ i) are constructed using the form mentioned in (1) with the SoftMax activation of the output layer, as well as ReLU activations in the hidden layers.

sections.summary: Implementation details for TNG classifiers, goal-reaching, and controllers. Trajectory classifiers use MobileNetV2 plus MLP and cross-entropy. Intersection recognition and goal reaching use a proprietary object recognition engine with FAST and BRIEF to reduce manual labelling. Regression controller architecture is an MLP with clipped output; object-detection controller uses 896×360 pixel bounding boxes and clipped PID output on SentiBotics.

source_span.start_text: Our implementation of trajectory imitation controllers and TNG is performed with the use of Neurotechnology’s SentiBotics Navigation SDK 3.0 [20].

sections.summary: Evaluates the two trajectory imitation controllers. Describes real environments L1-L3 and simulated L4, data collection by driving each trajectory three times, controller training, ten-lap closed-loop tests, percentage autonomy metric, and a second evaluation after four weeks. Results show near-perfect simulation performance, stronger initial regression scores but greater degradation over time, and better environmental tolerance and fewer cascading errors for the object-detection controller.
sections.title: Evaluating Trajectory Imitation Controllers

source_span.end_text: On the other side, the proposed TNG approach assumes that the navigation environment should consist of separable, intersecting trajectories.
source_span.start_text: We cover a subset of an office environment with five trajectories (denoted as T1-T5), and construct the corresponding TNG, as depicted in Figure 7.

sections.summary: Tests TNG navigation in an office environment with five trajectories T1-T5. For each source-destination pair, runs autonomous episodes and records percentage autonomy, travelled distance, and initial/goal/final images. Results indicate TNG can compose reactive controllers into goal-directed navigation. Discussion compares TNG with metric, topological, and hybrid approaches; highlights modularity, incremental augmentation, and system-level interpretability, but notes assumptions of separable intersecting trajectories, geometric sub-optimality, and significant human effort.
sections.title: TNG Navigation Experiments and Discussion

source_span.end_text: Our future work will include research on more efficient and reliable imitation learning approaches able to handle more dynamic environments, optimising TNG by adding a fully automatic environment graph construction capability and extending it with a hierarchical component.
source_span.start_text: In this article, we studied how to utilise reactive trajectory imitation controllers for topological, goal-directed autonomous robot navigation.

sections.summary: Concludes that neural object detection architectures can be applied efficiently to visuomotor trajectory imitation and that TNG can compose reactive trajectory imitation modules into a goal-directed navigation system. Future work includes more efficient and reliable imitation learning for dynamic environments, automatic graph construction, and a hierarchical component.
sections.title: Conclusion and Future Work

abstract.text: We focus on the utilisation of reactive trajectory imitation controllers for goal-directed mobile robot navigation. We propose a topological navigation graph (TNG) - an imitationlearning-based framework for navigating through environments with intersecting trajectories. The TNG framework represents the environment as a directed graph composed of deep neural networks. Each vertex of the graph corresponds to a trajectory and is represented by a trajectory identification classifier and a trajectory imitation controller. For trajectory following, we propose the novel use of neural object detection architectures. The edges of TNG correspond to intersections between trajectories and are all represented by a classifier. We provide empirical evaluation of the proposed navigation framework and its components in simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating that TNG allows us to utilise non-goal-directed, imitation-learning methods for goal-directed autonomous navigation.

source_span.start_text: Combining perception and action into a single algorithm of fundamental and practical importance, mobile robot navigation is an attractive area for artificial intelligence research.

sections.summary: Motivates the need for goal-directed navigation from imitation-learning components. Reviews the limitations of probabilistic-geometric models and the promise of neural-network imitation learning, then identifies the core problem that many imitation-learning algorithms are not goal-directed by design. Introduces the TNG framework as the solution and lists the paper’s main contributions.
sections.title: Introduction: Goal-Directed Navigation from Imitation Learning

source_span.end_text: The error input for the PID controller is defined as e t:= x t − x c, where x t and x c are the detected bounding box’s centre x coordinate and the centre x coordinate of the input image (see Figure 3).
source_span.start_text: In this section, we focus on learning a reactive skill of visuomotor trajectory following independently from the overall navigation method.

sections.summary: Defines the trajectory-following skill and presents two reactive controllers. The regression controller uses a fixed CNN encoder with a trainable MLP, ridge regression, DAgger, and augmentation; its limitations are rotational error sensitivity, environmental sensitivity, and weak correlation between offline loss and execution. The object-detection-based controller uses RetinaNet to detect the direction of movement as a single-class bounding box, then a PID controller centers the box.
sections.title: Trajectory Imitation Controllers: Regression and Object Detection

source_span.start_text: In this section, we review similar work of other authors and formally describe the proposed TNG framework for creating a goal-driven navigation system from separately learnt reactive skills.

sections.summary: Reviews related navigation approaches: mapper-planner end-to-end methods, semi-parametric topological memory, and kilometre-scale reinforcement-learning navigation. Critiques their resource demands, assumptions, or lack of real-world demonstrations. Then formally defines TNG as a directed graph whose vertices are trajectory imitation controllers plus trajectory classifiers and whose edges are intersection classifiers. Describes localisation, goal identification, shortest-path planning, switching, and goal reaching.

sections.summary: Implementation details for TNG classifiers, goal-reaching, and controllers. Trajectory classifiers use MobileNetV2 plus MLP and cross-entropy. Intersection recognition and goal reaching use a proprietary object recognition engine with FAST and BRIEF to reduce manual labelling. Regression controller architecture is an MLP with clipped output; object-detection controller uses 896×360 pixel bounding boxes and clipped PID output on SentiBotics.

sections.summary: Evaluates the two trajectory imitation controllers. Describes real environments L1-L3 and simulated L4, data collection by driving each trajectory three times, controller training, ten-lap closed-loop tests, percentage autonomy metric, and a second evaluation after four weeks. Results show near-perfect simulation performance, stronger initial regression scores but greater degradation over time, and better environmental tolerance and fewer cascading errors for the object-detection controller.

sections.summary: Tests TNG navigation in an office environment with five trajectories T1-T5. For each source-destination pair, runs autonomous episodes and records percentage autonomy, travelled distance, and initial/goal/final images. Results indicate TNG can compose reactive controllers into goal-directed navigation. Discussion compares TNG with metric, topological, and hybrid approaches; highlights modularity, incremental augmentation, and system-level interpretability, but notes assumptions of separable intersecting trajectories, geometric sub-optimality, and significant human effort.

sections.summary: Concludes that neural object detection architectures can be applied efficiently to visuomotor trajectory imitation and that TNG can compose reactive trajectory imitation modules into a goal-directed navigation system. Future work includes more efficient and reliable imitation learning for dynamic environments, automatic graph construction, and a hierarchical component.
